tagline.text: A Virgin Mary shrine rock off Station 1, the symbol of Boracay

location.label: Location
location.text: Station 1, White Beach, Balabag, Boracay Island, Malay, Aklan

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (viewing the rock is free; the cost of getting to Boracay is separate)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Caticlan Airport (MPH, Godofredo P. Ramos Airport) or Kalibo International Airport (KLO)

children.text: Willy's Rock is a volcanic rock formation on the shore at Station 1 of Boracay's White Beach, topped by a small Virgin Mary shrine. It is free to see at any hour, and at low tide you can walk right up to it, which makes it a favorite sunset photo spot.

Willy's Rock rises from the spot where sand meets sea in front of Station 1, near the northern end of White Beach. From a distance it looks like a big battleship, and a small shrine to the Virgin Mary stands on the tallest rock. Because it appears so often in photos, souvenirs, and tumblers about Boracay, it is called a symbol of the island.

The most widely repeated explanation is that the rock is named after Willy's Beach Club Hotel, which sits directly across from it. Locals also tell a story that the name comes from the hotel's founder, but that has not been confirmed in writing. Local Catholic residents placed the Virgin Mary statue on the rock and are said to have built steps so that visitors would not get hurt on the jagged surfaces. A Boracay local publication ran a photo from 1994 and noted that the rock was just starting to become a popular tourist spot around then.

The rock is close to the shoreline, so at low tide you can walk across the sand to its base, while at high tide the water rises and you need to wade, swim, or snorkel to reach it. The distance to the rock is described as roughly 50–100 m depending on the tide. Local worshippers leave flowers and candles at the shrine and look after it, so remember that this is a photo spot and a place of faith at the same time.

There is not much here to keep you for long. Thirty minutes is enough to see everything, and most travelers drop by on an early-morning walk or at sunset, take their photos, and move on. Station 1 is, however, the widest stretch of sand on White Beach and home to upscale resorts, so you can walk the beach around the rock and combine it with parau sailing and a café stop for a half-day outing. Boracay's beaches have been managed more strictly since the major environmental clean-up of 2018. Beach rules can change, so check the latest notices, and do not litter around the rock or pull plants from it.

blocks.title: Virgin Mary shrine on the rock

children.text: A statue of the Virgin Mary stands on the upper part of the largest rock, and flowers and candles are placed there. Local worshippers tend the space regularly, so avoid loud noise and do not climb up to mess around. Approach the shrine closely only at low tide.

blocks.title: Walking to the base at low tide

children.text: At low tide a path between the sand and the rock is exposed, and you can walk right up to its base. At high tide, on the other hand, the rock looks as if it were rising out of the sea, which photographs well. Check the tide table first if you want to see both looks in one day.

Seen from the beach, the three large rocks and the trees and shrubs on top are often said to look like a single battleship. Take your landscape shots from a few steps away to bring out this silhouette.

White Beach faces west, so at sunset the rock turns into a backlit silhouette. When a parau sailboat passes at the right moment, it becomes the classic Boracay photo. The number of people taking pictures grows from about an hour before sunset.

blocks.title: A quiet beach at early morning

children.text: Around 6 a.m. there are few people and the sea floor under the rock is clearly visible. When the tide cooperates you can climb the steps to the shrine and shoot from close up, which is why photo enthusiasts recommend this hour.

Station 1 is the widest stretch of sand on White Beach. Walking south from the rock takes you past a continuous line of beach resorts and cafés, and to the north a quiet coastal path leads toward Diniwid. Station 1 also has upscale resorts such as Discovery Shores, which gives the whole beach a tidy atmosphere.

Right beside the rock there are beach drink stands, including a shop known for tropical fruit shakes. They make a good rest stop to cool off after sightseeing. Check on the spot whether they are open and what they charge.

items.title: Sunset photo route
items.subtitle: How to spend an afternoon at Station 1

children.text: Arrive at the Station 1 beach and check the
tide table
. At low tide it is a good time to walk to the base of the rock.
Walk to the foot of Willy's Rock and look at the Virgin Mary statue and the steps up close. Non-slip sandals or water shoes are safest.
Step back from the rock, pick a spot for landscape photos, and face the direction where the sun will set. About an hour before sunset is when spots are least crowded.
Depending on the season, sunset falls roughly between 17:30 and 18:20, so wait until the parau sailboats pass.
After sunset, head to the beachfront restaurants at Stations 1–2 for dinner.
Sunset times are rough figures that vary by season. Check an exact time with a sunset app or at your hotel.

items.title: Early morning route
items.subtitle: Photos of the rock without the crowds

children.text: Walk out to the beach from your Station 2 hotel and head to Station 1. It takes only a few minutes.
At low tide, go right up to the base of the rock and photograph the shrine. At this hour hardly anyone offers to take your photo for a fee.
Have a fruit shake or coffee at a beach café and head back to your hotel.
At high tide the rock is surrounded by water and you cannot get close. In that case, take only wide shots from the beach.

From Cagban Port to Station 1 on White Beach, take an electric tricycle or a shared ride. The fare depends on the number of passengers and on negotiation, so check on the spot.
Stations 1–3 can be covered on foot along the beach. From Station 2 to Willy's Rock is a few minutes along the beach path.
You can see Willy's Rock all year, but the best time to walk to its base is when the dry season and low tide coincide. Sunset photos come out best in the dry season when there are few clouds.

One blog noted that in the so-called "ber" months starting in November there is less seaweed and the bottom around the rock is clearly visible. During the day, early morning or an hour before sunset brings fewer people and better photos.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Clear and relatively cool, calm sea
Little seaweed keeps the area around the rock clean, and it is the best season for sunset photos.
The beach is crowded, so go in the early morning or just before sunset.
Rainy season with frequent rain and wind
Waves and seaweed can increase on the west-facing White Beach, and many days the sunset is hidden by cloud.

Station 1 is the widest stretch of sand on White Beach and has many upscale resorts. Accommodation near Willy's Rock lets you walk out early in the morning to take photos, and prices run higher than at Stations 2 and 3. To save money, you can stay at Station 2 or 3 and walk over along the beach path.

Restaurants and bars are most concentrated around D'Mall at Station 2, while around the rock there are beach cafés and fruit shake stands. At sunset the beachfront restaurants fill up fast, so book ahead or arrive early. Shop names and prices change often, so check on the spot.

For a family trip, keep the time at the rock short and spend the rest on beach swimming and the hotel pool. With children, even shallow water near the rock can suddenly turn deep at high tide, so hold their hands as you move. With older travelers, a short outing that walks the beach path from a Station 1 hotel to see the rock is the least tiring. Since sunset is the busiest time, another good option is to look at the rock from a distance while having dinner on a hotel balcony or at a beachfront restaurant.
Check the tide table first. If you time it for low tide, you can walk right to the base of the rock.
The rock is slippery, so wear water shoes or non-slip sandals rather than going barefoot.
It is a shrine, so avoid loud noise, fooling around on the rock, and exaggerated poses in front of the statue.
Some reviews mention people who take photos in front of the statue and then ask for money. If you did not ask for it, you can politely decline.
For sunset photos, step back from the rock and shoot wide to capture the parau sailboats along with it.
To watch the sunset, claim your spot about an hour before the sun goes down.
If you want a quieter sunset, the beaches toward Diniwid and Puka are good alternatives.
Check the iPass notices for Boracay's entry fees and environmental rules before you leave.
The rock silhouette is sharpest in the roughly 20 minutes after sunset while the blue sky remains, so wait a little longer instead of leaving right away.
A waterproof phone case or a zip bag gives peace of mind if a wave suddenly reaches you on the low-tide path.
At high tide the water around the rock rises quickly. Check the tide times so that you do not walk out at low tide and then fail to get back in time.
The rock surface is very slippery when wet and its edges are sharp, so cuts are easy to get.
The steps and railings at the shrine are narrow, so it is dangerous if many people climb at once.
Boracay has beach touts and people who demand payment for photos, so confirm the price first.
On rainy days or when the waves are high, do not go near the rock.
Belongings often go missing on the beach around sunset, so keep valuables on your person.
